title: Ferenand getrü und Ferenand ungetrü
titleEn: Ferdinand the Faithful and Ferdinand the Unfaithful
part: Ferdinand the Faithful and Ferdinand the Unfaithful
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 126. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch); the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form.
about: KHM 126, told entirely in Low German, sets a loyal young man against a rival who happens to share almost his name: Ferenand getrü, given a magic white horse by his beggar godfather, and Ferenand ungetrü, who keeps talking the king into sending him on errands meant to kill him — fetching a sleeping princess past giants and hungry birds, then recovering a letter dropped in open water. Small kindnesses along the way, to a stranded fish among others, come back to save him each time, and the tale closes with a beheading trick that the new queen turns on the king who wronged him, clearing her way to marry Ferenand instead.

sentences.t: Et was mal en Mann un ’ne Fru west, de hadden so lange se rick wören kene Kinner, as se awerst arm woren, da kregen se en kleinen Jungen.
sentences.l: There was once a man and a wife, they had, so long as they were rich, no children; but when they grew poor, then they got a little boy.
sentences.i: There were once a man and his wife who, so long as they were rich, had no children; but when they grew poor, a little boy was born to them.
sentences.n: This whole tale is told in Low German (Plattdeutsch), the old speech of the north — narration and all, not only the speeches; the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form. The regular swaps begin here: Et = es, was … west = ist gewesen, un = und, ’ne Fru = eine Frau, de = die, kene Kinner = keine Kinder, rick = reich, woren = wurden, kregen = kriegten (bekamen).

sentences.t: Se kunnen awerst kenen Paen dato kregen, da segde de Mann, he wulle mal na den annern Ohre (Orte) gahn un tosehn ob he da enen krege.
sentences.l: But they could get no godfather for it, so the man said he would go once to the other place and see whether he might get one there.
sentences.i: But they could find no godfather for him, so the man said he would go over to the next village and see whether he could get one there.
sentences.n: A child needed a godfather before it could be christened, and a poor man’s difficulty in finding one sets the story going. “(Orte)” in round brackets is the Grimms’ own gloss, printed in the 1857 text to explain the dialect word Ohre to their readers — a dozen more of theirs follow in this tale. “segde” = sagte; “wulle” = wollte; “gahn” = gehen; “krege” is the past subjunctive of reported speech, “might get.”

sentences.t: Wie he so gienk, begegnete ünn en armen Mann, de frog en wo he hünne wulle,
sentences.l: As he went along so, a poor man met him, who asked him where he would go,
sentences.i: As he was walking along, a poor man met him and asked him where he was bound,
sentences.n: “begegnen” takes the dative — the man meets “to him,” so ünn here is ihm rather than ihn. “frog” = fragte; “hünne” = hin. The telling slips between past and present tense all through this tale; that is the storyteller’s voice, not an error.

sentences.t: he segde he wulle hünn un tosehn dat he ’n Paen kriegte, he sie arm, un da wulle ünn ken Minske to Gevaher stahn.
sentences.l: he said he would go there and see that he got a godfather; he was poor, and so no person would stand godfather to him.
sentences.i: he said he was going there to see about getting a godfather; he was poor, and no one would stand godfather for him.
sentences.n: “he sie arm” is the subjunctive of reported speech — the teller passes the words on without vouching for them, which English marks with “he said.” “to Gevaher stahn” = zu Gevatter stehen, to stand as godparent; Gevatter is the old word for the bond between parents and godparents. “Minske” = Mensch.

sentences.t: „O,“ segde de arme Mann, „gi sied arm, un ik sie arm, ik will guhe (euer) Gevaher weren;
sentences.l: “Oh,” said the poor man, “you are poor, and I am poor, I will be your godfather;
sentences.i: “Oh,” said the poor man, “you are poor and I am poor — I will be your child’s godfather;
sentences.n: “gi sied” = ihr seid: the beggar addresses him as “ihr,” the older respectful you. “(euer)” is again the Grimms’ own gloss, here on the dialect guhe. “weren” = werden, to become.

sentences.t: ik sie awerst so arm, ik kann dem Kinne nix giwen,
sentences.l: but I am so poor, I can give the child nothing,
sentences.i: but I am so poor that I can give the child nothing,
sentences.n: “dem Kinne” is dem Kinde, the dative of Kind — the one given to. (Elsewhere in the collection this same spelling stands for können; here it is plainly the child.) “giwen” = geben; “nix” = nichts.

sentences.t: gahet hen un segget de Bähmoer (Wehmutter) se sulle man mit den Kinne na der Kerken kummen.“
sentences.l: go along and tell the midwife she should just come with the child to the church.”
sentences.i: go along and tell the midwife to come to the church with the child.”
sentences.n: “(Wehmutter)” is the Grimms’ own gloss once more: a Bähmoer is the midwife, in older High German Wehmutter, the woman who attends a birth. Low German “man” means nur, only, just — not the impersonal High German man. “sulle” is the subjunctive of reported speech.

sentences.t: Ase se nu tohaupe an der Kerken kummet, da is de Bettler schaun darinne, de givt dem Kinne den Namen Ferenand getrü.
sentences.l: When they now come together to the church, the beggar is already inside; he gives the child the name Ferenand getrü.
sentences.i: When they came to the church together, the beggar was already inside, and he gave the child the name Ferenand getrü.
sentences.n: Ferenand getrü is Ferdinand the faithful. The names are left in their dialect form throughout, and the counterpart Ferenand ungetrü — the unfaithful — turns up later; between them the two names hold the whole moral scheme of the tale. “tohaupe” = zuhauf, together; “schaun” = schon; “darinne” = darin.

sentences.t: Wie he nu ut der Kerken gahet, da segd de Bettler, „nu gahet man na Hus, ik kann guh (euch) nix giwen un gi süllt mi ok nix giwen.“
sentences.l: As they now go out of the church, the beggar says, “now just go home, I can give you nothing and you shall give me nothing either.”
sentences.i: As they came out of the church, the beggar said: “Now go home; I can give you nothing, and you shall give me nothing either.”
sentences.n: “he … gahet” puts a singular pronoun with a plural verb — the sense is clearly “as they go out,” and the loose fit is the spoken telling showing through. “(euch)” is the Grimms’ own gloss on guh; “ok” = auch; “süllt” = sollt.

sentences.t: De Bähmoer awerst gav he ’n Schlüttel un segd er se mögt en, wenn se na Hus käme, dem Vaer giwen,
sentences.l: But to the midwife he gave a key and said to her she might give it, when she came home, to the father,
sentences.i: But he gave the midwife a key and told her to give it to the father when she got home,
sentences.n: “De Bähmoer” stands first although she is the one given to; Low German does not mark the dative here, so word order and sense have to carry it. “er” in this sentence is ihr, to her — not er, he. “mögt” is the reported-speech subjunctive of mögen.

sentences.t: de sull’n verwahren, bis dat Kind vertein Johr old wöre,
sentences.l: he should keep it safe until the child was fourteen years old,
sentences.i: and he was to keep it safe until the child was fourteen years old,
sentences.n: “de” is the demonstrative der, “that one” — the father. “sull’n” = sollte ihn, with the pronoun swallowed into the verb; the apostrophe marks what has dropped out. “vertein Johr” = vierzehn Jahr.

sentences.t: dann sull et up de Heide gahn, da wöre ’n Schlott, dato paßte de Schlüttel,
sentences.l: then it should go onto the heath, there would be a castle, to which the key fitted,
sentences.i: then the child was to go out onto the heath, where there would be a castle that the key fitted,
sentences.n: “et” is the child (Kind is neuter). “Schlott” is das Schloß, a castle — and the same German word also means a lock, which is why key and castle sit together so naturally here. The verbs stay in the subjunctive: this is all still the beggar’s instruction, reported.

sentences.t: wat darin wöre, dat sulle em hören.
sentences.l: what was in it, that should belong to him.
sentences.i: and whatever was inside should belong to him.
sentences.n: “hören” here is gehören, to belong; Low German drops the ge-. The what/that pair — “wat … dat” — is how older German holds the two halves together where English says “whatever.”

sentences.t: Wie dat Kind nu sewen Johr alt wor, un düet (tüchtig) wassen wor, gienk et mal spilen mit annern Jungens,
sentences.l: When the child was now seven years old, and had grown sturdily, it went once to play with other boys,
sentences.i: When the child was seven years old and had grown sturdily, he went out once to play with other boys,
sentences.n: “(tüchtig)” is the Grimms’ own gloss on düet: soundly, in good earnest. “wassen wor” = gewachsen war; “wor” = war. “spilen” = spielen.

sentences.t: da hadde de eine noch mehr vom Paen kriegt, ase de annere, he awerst kunne nix seggen,
sentences.l: then the one had got still more from his godfather than the other, but he could say nothing,
sentences.i: and one boy had had more from his godfather than another, but he had nothing to tell,
sentences.n: Godparents gave gifts, and the boys are comparing them. “ase” here is als, than; “kunne” = konnte.

sentences.t: un da grinde he un gienk nah Hus un segde tom Vaer „hewe ik denn gar nix vom Paen kriegt?“
sentences.l: and then he wept and went home and said to his father “have I then got nothing at all from my godfather?”
sentences.i: and so he cried, and went home, and said to his father: “Have I then had nothing at all from my godfather?”
sentences.n: “grinen” in Low German is weinen, to cry — it has nothing to do with modern grinsen, to grin, and it is one of the easiest dialect words to misread. “hewe” = habe; “nah Hus” = nach Haus.

sentences.t: „O ja,“ segde de Vaer, „du hest en Schlüttel kriegt, wenn up de Heide ’n Schlott steit, so gah man hen un schlut et up.“
sentences.l: “Oh yes,” said the father, “you have got a key; if a castle stands on the heath, then just go there and unlock it.”
sentences.i: “Oh yes,” said the father, “you were given a key; if there is a castle standing on the heath, then go and unlock it.”
sentences.n: “hest” = hast; “steit” = steht; “schlut … up” = schließ auf, the separable aufschließen with its particle at the end. “man” is again “just, only.”

sentences.t: Da gienk he hen, awerst et was kein Schlott to hören un to sehen.
sentences.l: Then he went there, but there was no castle to hear and to see.
sentences.i: So he went, but there was no castle to be heard of or seen.
sentences.n: “to hören un to sehen” doubles the two senses to mean “no sign of it at all” — German pairs them where English would use one.

sentences.t: Wier na sewen Jahren, ase he vertein Johr old is, geit he nochmals hen, da steit en Schlott darup.
sentences.l: Again after seven years, when he is fourteen years old, he goes there once more, and a castle stands on it.
sentences.i: Seven years later, when he was fourteen, he went again, and there stood a castle on the heath.
sentences.n: The tale counts in sevens — seven years, then fourteen — the usual measure in these stories. “darup” = darauf, on it, meaning on the heath.

sentences.t: Wie he et upschloten het, da is der nix enne, ase ’n Perd, ’n Schümmel.
sentences.l: When he has unlocked it, there is nothing in it but a horse, a white horse.
sentences.i: When he had unlocked it, there was nothing inside but a horse — a white one.
sentences.n: A Schümmel (Schimmel) is a white or grey horse; this one is the tale’s second hero, and will turn out to be a good deal more than a horse. “upschloten” = aufgeschlossen; “enne” = drinnen; “ase” here is als in the sense “but, except.”

sentences.t: Da werd de Junge so vuller Früden dat he dat Perd hadde, dat he sik darup sett un to sinen Vaer jegd (jagt).
sentences.l: Then the boy becomes so full of joy that he had the horse, that he sets himself on it and gallops to his father.
sentences.i: The boy was so full of joy at having the horse that he sat himself on it and galloped off to his father.
sentences.n: “(jagt)” is the Grimms’ own gloss on the dialect jegd — he races, gallops. “vuller Früden” = voller Freuden; “sett” here is the plain third person setzt, not an imperative.

sentences.t: „Nu hew ik auck ’n Schümmel, nu will ik auck reisen“ segd he.
sentences.l: “Now I have a white horse too, now I will travel too,” says he.
sentences.i: “Now I too have a horse; now I too will go travelling,” he said.
sentences.n: “hew” = habe; “auck” = auch. Going out into the world is what a young man with a horse does in these tales, and the horse is what makes it possible.

sentences.t: Da treckt he weg, un wie he unnerweges is, ligd da ’ne Schriffedder up ’n Wegge,
sentences.l: Then he draws away, and as he is on the road, a writing-quill lies there in the way,
sentences.i: So he set off, and as he was on the road, there lay a writing-quill in the way,
sentences.n: “trecken” = ziehen, and wegtrecken is to set off — the same drawing-away German uses of a journey. A Schriffedder is die Schreibfeder, the quill; it will matter twice more before the tale is done.

sentences.t: he will se eist (erst) upnümmen,
sentences.l: he wants at first to pick it up,
sentences.i: at first he meant to pick it up,
sentences.n: “(erst)” is the Grimms’ own gloss on eist. “upnümmen” = aufnehmen, to take up.

sentences.t: da denkt he awerst wier bie sich „o, du süst se auck liggen laten, du findst ja wul, wo du hen kümmst, ’ne Schriffedder, wenn du eine bruckest.“
sentences.l: but then he thinks again to himself “oh, you shall let it lie as well, you will surely find a writing-quill wherever you come, if you need one.”
sentences.i: but then he thought better of it: “Oh, you may as well leave it lying; wherever you go you will surely find a quill if you need one.”
sentences.n: He talks to himself as “du,” which the tales do whenever someone weighs a thing up. “süst” here is sollst; later in this same tale the identical spelling stands for sonst, otherwise — only the sentence can tell you which. “bruckest” = brauchst.

sentences.t: Wie he so weggeit, do roppt et hinner üm „Ferenand getrü, nümm se mit.“
sentences.l: As he so goes away, it calls behind him “Ferenand getrü, take it with you.”
sentences.i: As he was going off, a voice called behind him: “Ferenand getrü, take it with you.”
sentences.n: “et roppt” — “it calls”: the impersonal es is how German reports a voice with no visible speaker, where English says “a voice called.” “üm” here is ihm, him.

sentences.t: He süt sik ümme, süt awerst keinen, da geit he wier torugge un nümmt se up.
sentences.l: He looks himself around, but sees no one; then he goes back again and takes it up.
sentences.i: He looked about him but saw no one, so he went back and picked it up.
sentences.n: “sik ümme sehn” = sich umsehen, to look about one; ümme is the particle um, not the preposition. “torugge” = zurück.

sentences.t: Wie he wier ’ne Wile rien (geritten) is, kümmt he bie ’n Water vorbie, so ligd da en Fisk am Oewer (Ufer) un snappet un happet na Luft;
sentences.l: When he has ridden a while again, he comes past a water, and there lies a fish on the bank and snaps and gasps for air;
sentences.i: When he had ridden a while longer he came past a stretch of water, and there lay a fish on the bank, snapping and gasping for air;
sentences.n: Two of the Grimms’ own glosses stand in this one sentence: “(geritten)” on rien and “(Ufer)” on Oewer. “snappet un happet” is a sound-pair — snapping and gaping — of the kind the dialect likes.

sentences.t: so segd he „töv, min lewe Fisk, ik will die helpen, dat du in’t Water kümmst,“ un gript ’n bie’n Schwans un werpt ’n in’t Water.
sentences.l: so he says “wait, my dear fish, I will help you, that you come into the water,” and grasps it by the tail and throws it into the water.
sentences.i: so he said: “Wait, my dear fish, I will help you into the water,” and he took it by the tail and threw it in.
sentences.n: “töv” = warte, wait (töven = warten). In this tale “die” is dir or dich, you — not the article die; “in’t” = in dat, into the. Helping the creature met on the road is the move that always pays in these tales.

sentences.t: Da steckt de Fisk den Kopp ut den Water un segd „nu du mie ut den Koth holpen hest, will ik die ’ne Flötenpiepen giwen,
sentences.l: Then the fish sticks its head out of the water and says “now that you have helped me out of the mud, I will give you a little flute,
sentences.i: Then the fish put its head out of the water and said: “Now that you have helped me out of the mud, I will give you a little flute,
sentences.n: “nu” at the head of a clause means “now that” — a causal use. “Koth” is Kot, mud or filth (1857 spelling with th); “holpen” = geholfen.

sentences.t: wenn du in de Naud bist, so flöte derup, dann will ik die helpen,
sentences.l: when you are in need, then pipe on it, then I will help you,
sentences.i: if ever you are in need, pipe on it, and I will help you,
sentences.n: “Naud” is die Noth (modern Not), distress or hard straits. “flöte” is the imperative — pipe, blow; “derup” = darauf.

sentences.t: un wenn du mal wat in Water hest fallen laten, so flöte man, so will ik et die herut reicken.“
sentences.l: and if you have ever let something fall into the water, then just pipe, and I will hand it out to you.”
sentences.i: and if you should ever let something fall into the water, only pipe, and I will hand it out to you.”
sentences.n: “fallen laten” = fallen lassen, to let fall, to drop. “man” once more for nur, only. The second half of the promise sets up something that happens a long way further on.

sentences.t: Nu ritt he weg, da kümmt so ’n Minsk to üm, de frägt ’n wo he hen wull.
sentences.l: Now he rides away; then such a fellow comes to him, who asks him where he would go.
sentences.i: Now he rode on, and a man came up to him who asked him where he was bound.
sentences.n: “so ’n Minsk” — “such a person” — is the vague article a spoken tale uses to bring a stranger on stage; English does it with “a man came up.” “frägt” = fragt.

sentences.t: „O, na den neggsten Ohre.“ Wu he dann heite? „Ferenand getrü.“
sentences.l: “Oh, to the next place.” What then was he called? “Ferenand getrü.”
sentences.i: “Oh, to the next village.” And what was his name? “Ferenand getrü.”
sentences.n: The middle question is reported rather than quoted, and stands in the subjunctive (“heite” = hieße); the teller keeps the exchange running without a speech tag, which is why the two quoted answers sit on either side of it. “Wu” = wie; “neggsten” = nächsten.

sentences.t: „Sü, da hewe wie ja fast den sülwigen Namen, ik heite Ferenand ungetrü.“
sentences.l: “See, there we have almost the selfsame name, I am called Ferenand ungetrü.”
sentences.i: “See there, we have almost the very same name — I am called Ferenand ungetrü.”
sentences.n: “wie” here is wir, we — not the wie that means how or as; the one spelling does both jobs in this tale. Ferenand ungetrü is Ferdinand the unfaithful: the name says in advance exactly what he will do, and the tale never pretends otherwise.

sentences.t: Da trecket se beide na den neggsten Ohre in dat Wertshus.
sentences.l: Then they both draw to the next place, into the inn.
sentences.i: So the two of them went on to the next village, to the inn.
sentences.n: “Wertshus” = das Wirtshaus, the inn.

sentences.t: Nu was et schlimm, dat de Ferenand ungetrü allet wuste wat ’n annerer dacht hadde un doen wulle;
sentences.l: Now it was bad that Ferenand ungetrü knew everything that another had thought and meant to do;
sentences.i: Now the bad thing was that Ferenand ungetrü knew everything another man had thought or meant to do;
sentences.n: “dacht hadde” = gedacht hatte, had thought — dacht here is the participle of denken, not the noun Docht. “allet” = alles; “doen” = thun (modern tun).

sentences.t: dat wust he döre so allerhand slimme Kunste.
sentences.l: that he knew through all sorts of wicked arts.
sentences.i: and this he knew by all manner of wicked arts.
sentences.n: “döre” is durch, through, by means of. “Kunste” are arts in the old sense — skills — and here black ones; the tale gives no more explanation than that.

sentences.t: Et was awerst im Wertshuse so ’n wacker Mäken, dat hadde ’n schier (klares) Angesicht un drog sik so hübsch;
sentences.l: But there was in the inn such a fine girl, she had a clear face and carried herself so prettily;
sentences.i: But at the inn there was a fine girl with a clear face, and she carried herself prettily;
sentences.n: “(klares)” is the Grimms’ own gloss on schier. “Mäken” = Mädchen and is neuter, so the German says “dat” and “dat hadde” of her. “sik dragen” = sich tragen, to bear oneself.

sentences.t: dat verleiv sik in den Ferenand getrü, denn et was ’n hübschen Minschen west, un frog’n wo he hen to wulle.
sentences.l: she fell in love with Ferenand getrü, for he was a handsome fellow, and asked him where he wanted to go to.
sentences.i: she fell in love with Ferenand getrü, for he was a handsome fellow, and she asked him where he was making for.
sentences.n: “verleiv sik” = verliebte sich. “west” here is gewesen — but watch the same spelling further on, where “west du nig” is weißt du nicht, do you not know. “frog’n” = fragte ihn.

sentences.t: „O, he wulle so herümmer reisen.“
sentences.l: “Oh, he wanted to travel about so.”
sentences.i: “Oh, he was for travelling about a while.”
sentences.n: His answer is put in quotation marks but reported in the third person (“he wulle”) — the teller does not change gear between direct and reported speech, and the marks stay where they are.

sentences.t: Da segd se so sull he doch nur da bliewen, et wöre hier to Lanne ’n Künig, de neime wull geren ’n Bedeenten oder ’n Vorrüter:
sentences.l: Then she says he should just stay there, there was here in the land a king who would gladly take a servant or an outrider:
sentences.i: Then she said he should stay where he was: there was a king here in this country who would gladly take on a manservant or an outrider;
sentences.n: A Vorreiter rode ahead of his master’s carriage — a place close to the horses, which is why it will matter to him. “to Lanne” = zu Lande; “neime” = nähme, would take.

sentences.t: dabie sulle he in Diensten gahn.
sentences.l: with him he should go into service.
sentences.i: he should take service there.
sentences.n: “in Dienste gahn” = in Dienst gehen, to enter service; “dabie” = dabei, with that, there.

sentences.t: He antworde he kunne nig gud so to einen hingahen un been sik an.
sentences.l: He answered he could not well go up to someone like that and offer himself.
sentences.i: He answered that he could hardly go up to a man like that and offer himself.
sentences.n: “been sik an” is bietet sich an — sich anbieten, to offer oneself; been here is the verb bieten, not Bein, a leg. “nig gud” = nicht gut, hardly.

sentences.t: Da segde dat Mäken „o, dat will ik dann schun dauen.“
sentences.l: Then the girl said “oh, I will do that then.”
sentences.i: Then the girl said: “Oh, I will see to that.”
sentences.n: “schun” = schon, a particle of reassurance that English carries by tone rather than by a word. “dauen” = thun, to do.

sentences.t: Un so gienk se auck stracks hen na den Künig un sehde ünn se wüste ünn ’n hübschen Bedeenten.
sentences.l: And so she went straightway to the king and told him she knew of a handsome servant for him.
sentences.i: And so she went straight to the king and told him she knew of a handsome manservant for him.
sentences.n: “sehde” = sagte; “wüste” = wüßte, the reported-speech subjunctive of wissen. Both instances of ünn here are ihm — to him, and for him.

sentences.t: Dat was de wol tofreen un leit ’n to sik kummen un wull ’n tom Bedeenten macken.
sentences.l: With that he was well content and let him come to him and wanted to make him his servant.
sentences.i: The king was well content with that, and had him come, and would have made him his manservant.
sentences.n: “Dat was de wol tofreen” puts the thing agreed to first and the person after: “that, he was content with.” “leit” = ließ; “’n” here is ihn, him.

sentences.t: He wull awerst leewer Vorrüter sin, denn wo sin Perd wöre, da möst he auck sin;
sentences.l: But he would rather be an outrider, for where his horse was, there he must be too;
sentences.n: “sin” does two jobs in one sentence: the first is sein, to be, the second the possessive sein, his. “möst” = müßte.

sentences.t: da mackt ’n de Künig tom Vorrüter.
sentences.l: so the king makes him his outrider.
sentences.i: so the king made him his outrider.
sentences.n: “tom Vorrüter macken” = zum Vorreiter machen; the zu marks what a person is made into.

sentences.t: Wie düt de Ferenand ungetrü gewahr wore, da segd he to den Mäken „töv, helpest du den an un mie nig?“
sentences.l: When Ferenand ungetrü became aware of this, he said to the girl “wait — you help him on and not me?”
sentences.i: When Ferenand ungetrü got wind of this, he said to the girl: “Wait now — you help him to a place and not me?”
sentences.n: “gewahr werden” is to become aware of, to notice. “anhelpen” = anhelfen, to help someone into a place. “töv” — wait — is the same word he used kindly to the fish; here it is a threat.

sentences.t: „O,“ segd dat Mäken, „ik will ’n auck anhelpen.“
sentences.l: “Oh,” says the girl, “I will help him on too.”
sentences.i: “Oh,” said the girl, “I will get him a place too.”
sentences.n: “’n” is again ihn, him — the clipped pronoun is everywhere in this tale.

sentences.t: Se dachte „den most du die tom Frünne wahren, denn he is nig to truen.“
sentences.l: She thought “that one you must keep as a friend for yourself, for he is not to be trusted.”
sentences.i: She thought to herself: “That one you had better keep as a friend, for he is not to be trusted.”
sentences.n: “wahren” here is bewahren, to keep or hold on to — not the adjective wahr, true. “nig to truen” = nicht zu trauen: the tale states his character plainly, and early.

sentences.t: Se geit alse vorm Künig stahn un beed ’n als Bedeenten an; dat is de Künig tofreen.
sentences.l: So she goes and stands before the king and offers him as a servant; with that the king is content.
sentences.i: So she went and stood before the king and offered him as a manservant, and the king was content with that.
sentences.n: “geit … stahn” — goes to stand — is a Low German turn where High German would say stellt sich. “alse” = also; “beed … an” = bietet an, the separable anbieten.

sentences.t: Wenn he nu also det Morgens den Heren antrock, da jammerte de jümmer „o wenn ik doch eist mine Leiveste bie mie hädde.“
sentences.l: Now when he dressed his master in the morning, the man would always lament “oh, if only I had my dearest here with me.”
sentences.i: Now when he dressed his master of a morning, the king would always be lamenting: “Oh, if only I had my dearest here with me.”
sentences.n: “wenn” with a past tense means “whenever,” a thing repeated. “det Morgens” = des Morgens, of a morning — an old genitive of time. “antrock” = zog an; “de” is the demonstrative, “that one,” meaning the king; “Leiveste” = Liebste.

sentences.t: De Ferenand ungetrü was awerst dem Ferenand getrü jümmer uppsettsig,
sentences.l: But Ferenand ungetrü was always set against Ferenand getrü,
sentences.i: But Ferenand ungetrü was forever working against Ferenand getrü,
sentences.n: “uppsettsig” = aufsässig, set against someone; “jümmer” = immer.

sentences.t: wie asso de Künig mal wier so jammerte, da segd he „Sie haben ja den Vorreiter, den schicken Sie hin, der muß sie herbeischaffen,
sentences.l: so as the king was lamenting again, he said “you have the outrider, send him there, he must fetch her,
sentences.i: and so, when the king was lamenting again, he said: “You have the outrider — send him; he must fetch her,
sentences.n: Here the tale drops out of Low German into High German for the courtier’s speech, and uses the polite “Sie haben … schicken Sie” besides: the language of the court set against the dialect of everything around it. The 1857 text moves between the two without a word of explanation, and so does this edition.

sentences.t: und wenn er es nicht thut, so muß ihm der Kopf vor die Füße gelegt werden.“
sentences.l: and if he does not do it, then his head must be laid before his feet.”
sentences.i: and if he does not do it, then his head must be laid at his feet.”
sentences.n: “jemandem den Kopf vor die Füße legen” is the old formula for beheading; the tales say it flatly, and it means exactly what it says. “thut” is the 1857 spelling of tut.

sentences.t: Do leit de Künig den Ferenand getrü to sik kummen un sehde üm he hädde da un da ’ne Leiveste,
sentences.l: Then the king had Ferenand getrü come to him and told him he had in such and such a place a dearest,
sentences.i: Then the king had Ferenand getrü brought before him and told him he had a sweetheart in such and such a place,
sentences.n: “da un da” = da und da, in such and such a place — the tale does not name it and does not need to. “hädde” is the subjunctive of reported speech.

sentences.t: de sull he ünn herschappen, wenn he dat nig deie, sull he sterwen.
sentences.l: her he should fetch him, and if he did not do it, he should die.
sentences.i: and he was to fetch her for him; and if he did not, he should die.
sentences.n: “herschappen” = herschaffen, to bring here, to procure. “deie” = täte, the past subjunctive of doen. The threat comes in the same breath as the errand, which is how these kings speak.

sentences.t: De Ferenand getrü gienk in Stall to sinen Schümmel un grinde un jammerde.
sentences.l: Ferenand getrü went into the stable to his white horse and wept and lamented.
sentences.n: “grinde” is wept, from grinen = weinen — the dialect word already met when he was a boy at his father’s door.

sentences.t: „O wat sin ik ’n unglücksch Minschenkind.“
sentences.l: “Oh what an unlucky child of man I am.”
sentences.i: “Oh, what an unlucky creature I am.”
sentences.n: “sin ik” = bin ich: in this tale sin is “to be” and “am,” and also the possessive “his,” all under one spelling. “Minschenkind” = Menschenkind, a child of man — a solemn old word for a human being.

sentences.t: Do röppet jeimes hinner üm „Ferdinand getreu, was weinst du?“
sentences.l: Then someone calls behind him “Ferdinand getreu, why do you weep?”
sentences.i: Then someone called behind him: “Ferdinand getreu, why are you weeping?”
sentences.n: The voice speaks High German, and gives the name in its High German form Ferdinand getreu — the first sign that whoever is speaking is not what the stable seems to hold. “jeimes” = jemand; “röppet” = ruft.

sentences.t: He süt sik um, süt awerst neimes, un jammerd jümmer fort „o min lewe Schümmelken, nu mot ik die verlaten, nu mot ik sterwen.“
sentences.l: He looks around him, but sees no one, and laments on and on “oh my dear little white horse, now I must leave you, now I must die.”
sentences.i: He looked about him but saw no one, and went on lamenting: “Oh my dear little horse, now I must leave you, now I must die.”
sentences.n: “neimes” = niemand. “Schümmelken” is the diminutive — the little white horse; the tenderness carried by that -ken ending is the whole point of the scene.

sentences.t: Do röppet et wier „Ferdinand getreu, was weinst du?“
sentences.l: Then it calls again “Ferdinand getreu, why do you weep?”
sentences.i: Then the voice called again: “Ferdinand getreu, why are you weeping?”
sentences.n: The question comes a second time, word for word: the doubling is how the tale marks that something uncanny is under way.

sentences.t: Do merket he eist dat dat sin Schümmelken dei, dat Fragen.
sentences.l: Then he first notices that his little white horse was doing that, the asking.
sentences.i: Only then did he notice that it was his little horse doing the asking.
sentences.n: “dat Fragen” — the infinitive used as a noun, “the asking,” hung on at the end to name what the horse was doing. “eist” = erst; “dei” = tat.

sentences.t: „Döst du dat, min Schümmelken, kannst du küren (reden)?“
sentences.l: “Do you do that, my little white horse, can you speak?”
sentences.i: “Is it you, my little horse — can you speak?”
sentences.n: “(reden)” is the Grimms’ own gloss on küren, the Low German word for speaking. “Döst du” = tust du.

sentences.t: Un segd wier „ik sull da un da hen, un sull de Brut halen, west du nig wie ik dat wol anfange.“
sentences.l: And says again “I am to go to such and such a place and fetch the bride; do you not know how I might set about it?”
sentences.i: And he said further: “I am to go to such and such a place and fetch the bride — do you not know how I should set about it?”
sentences.n: “west du nig” = weißt du nicht: here west is “you know,” though the same spelling stood for gewesen earlier in the tale. Only the sentence tells you which word it is, and this is one of the places where the dialect genuinely has to be read twice.

sentences.t: Do antwoerd dat Schümmelken „gah du na den Künig un segg wenn he die giwen wulle wat du hewen möstest, so wullest du se ünn schappen:
sentences.l: Then the little white horse answered “go you to the king and say, if he would give you what you must have, then you would fetch her for him:
sentences.i: Then the little horse answered: “Go to the king and tell him that if he will give you what you must have, you will bring her to him:
sentences.n: “hewen” here is haben, to have — elsewhere in the collection the same spelling means Himmel, heaven, and this tale is not using it that way. “wullest” and “möstest” are subjunctives: a bargain being reported rather than made.

sentences.t: wenn he die ’n Schipp vull Fleisk un ’n Schipp vull Brod giwen wulle, so sull et gelingen;
sentences.l: if he would give you a ship full of meat and a ship full of bread, then it should succeed;
sentences.i: if he will give you a ship full of meat and a ship full of bread, then it will succeed;
sentences.n: “Schipp” = Schiff; “Fleisk” = Fleisch; “Brod” is the 1857 spelling of Brot. Two shiploads are the whole plan, and the reason for them follows at once.

sentences.t: da wören de grauten Riesen up den Water, wenn du denen ken Fleisk midde brächtes, so terreitn se die:
sentences.l: there would be the great giants on the water, if you brought them no meat with you, they would tear you to pieces:
sentences.i: for the great giants are out on the water, and if you brought them no meat, they would tear you to pieces;
sentences.n: “midde” here is mit, along — “midde bringen” is mitbringen, to bring along — and not die Mitte, the middle. “terreitn” = zerrissen; “brächtes” = brächtest.

sentences.t: un da wören de grauten Vüggel, de pickeden die de Ogen ut den Koppe, wenn du ken Brod vor se häddest.“
sentences.l: and there would be the great birds, they would peck the eyes out of your head, if you had no bread for them.”
sentences.i: and there are the great birds, which would peck the eyes out of your head if you had no bread for them.”
sentences.n: “de pickeden die de Ogen ut den Koppe” — they would peck you the eyes out of the head: German marks the person harmed with a dative (die = dir) and leaves the body part under a plain article. Nothing here is softened, and nothing should be.

sentences.t: Da lett de Künig alle Slächter im Lanne slachten un alle Becker backen, dat de Schippe vull werdt.
sentences.l: Then the king has all the butchers in the land slaughter and all the bakers bake, so that the ships become full.
sentences.i: Then the king set all the butchers in the land to slaughtering and all the bakers to baking, until the ships were full.
sentences.n: “lett” here is läßt — to have a thing done — and not the Low German lett that means “looks, seems.” “Schippe” is the plural, ships; “Slächter” = Schlächter; “Becker” = Bäcker.

sentences.t: Wie se vull sied, segd dat Schümmelken tom Ferenand getrü „nu gah man up mie sitten un treck mit mie in’t Schipp,
sentences.l: When they are full, the little white horse says to Ferenand getrü “now just go and sit on me and draw with me into the ship,
sentences.i: When they were full, the little horse said to Ferenand getrü: “Now sit up on me and come aboard the ship with me,
sentences.n: “sied” is sind, are — not the High German seit, since. “treck mit mie” = zieh mit mir, come along with me.

sentences.t: wenn dann de Riesen kümmet, so segg
sentences.l: and when the giants come, then say
sentences.n: The sentence runs straight on into the rhyme below: the charm itself is the end of it, which is why there is no full stop here.

sentences.t:
„still, still, meine lieben Riesechen,
ich hab euch wohl bedacht,
ich hab euch was mitgebracht.“
sentences.l:
“still, still, my dear little giants,
I have kept you well in mind,
I have brought you something.”
sentences.i:
“Hush, hush, my dear little giants,
I have not forgotten you,
I have brought you something.”
sentences.n: The charm is in High German although the tale around it is Low German — spoken formulas often keep an older, more formal shape. It rhymes bedacht / mitgebracht, which the English does not try to reproduce. “Riesechen” is a diminutive of Riese: he calls the giants little giants, and the coaxing lies in that. “wohl bedacht” means both thought well of and provided for.

sentences.t: Un wenn de Vüggel kümmet, so seggst du wier
sentences.l: And when the birds come, then you say again
sentences.n: “Vüggel” = Vögel; “kümmet” = kommen. The instruction is the one before with a single word changed, and the rhyme that follows changes by a single word too.

sentences.t:
„still, still, meine lieben Vögelchen,
ich hab euch wohl bedacht,
ich hab euch was mitgebracht.“
sentences.l:
“still, still, my dear little birds,
I have kept you well in mind,
I have brought you something.”
sentences.i:
“Hush, hush, my dear little birds,
I have not forgotten you,
I have brought you something.”
sentences.n: As before, but Vögelchen — little birds — for Riesechen; everything else stands. The repetition is the form of the charm, not a slip of the printer’s.

sentences.t: Dann doet sie die nix, un wenn du dann bie dat Schlott kümmst, dann helpet die de Riesen,
sentences.l: Then they do you nothing, and when you then come to the castle, then the giants help you,
sentences.i: Then they will do you no harm; and when you come to the castle, the giants will help you,
sentences.n: “doet sie die nix” = tun sie dir nichts — die is dir here. “helpet” = helfen.

sentences.t: dann gah up dat Schlott un nümm ’n Paar Riesen mit, da ligd de Prinzessin un schlöppet;
sentences.l: then go up into the castle and take a couple of giants with you, there lies the princess and sleeps;
sentences.i: then go up into the castle and take a couple of giants with you; there the princess lies asleep;
sentences.n: “schlöppet” = schläft. German says “lies and sleeps” where English turns one of the two verbs into a participle.

sentences.t: du darfst se awerst nig upwecken, sonnern de Riesen mött se mit den Bedde upnümmen un in dat Schipp dregen.“
sentences.l: but you may not wake her, rather the giants must take her up with the bed and carry her into the ship.”
sentences.i: but you must not wake her; the giants must lift her up, bed and all, and carry her into the ship.”
sentences.n: “dürfen” is about permission — you may not, rather than you cannot. “mött” = müssen; “dregen” = tragen. Carrying her off asleep, bed and all, is this tale’s idea of an errand well done, and no one in it objects.

sentences.t: Und da geschah nun alles, wie das Schimmelchen gesagt hatte,
sentences.l: And then everything now happened as the little white horse had said,
sentences.i: And so it all came to pass as the little horse had said,
sentences.n: The narration itself switches to High German here for a stretch — “Schimmelchen” instead of Schümmelken — and will switch back again a few lines further on. The 1857 text is a patchwork of the two, and the seams are left where they are.

sentences.t: und den Riesen und den Vögeln gab der Ferenand getrü was er ihnen mitgebracht hatte, dafür wurden die Riesen willig und trugen die Prinzessin in ihrem Bett zum König.
sentences.l: and to the giants and the birds Ferenand getrü gave what he had brought them, and for that the giants became willing and carried the princess in her bed to the king.
sentences.i: and Ferenand getrü gave the giants and the birds what he had brought for them, and for that the giants grew willing and carried the princess in her bed to the king.
sentences.n: The two datives stand at the head — “den Riesen und den Vögeln gab der Ferenand getrü …” — which German can do freely, because the case endings and not the word order say who gives and who receives.

sentences.t: Un ase se tom Künig kümmet, segd se se künne nig liwen, se möste ere Schriften hewen, de wören up eren Schlotte liggen bliwen.
sentences.l: And when she comes to the king, she says she could not live, she must have her writings, they had stayed lying at her castle.
sentences.i: And when she came to the king, she said she could not live: she must have her writings, which had been left lying at her castle.
sentences.n: Back into Low German inside the same paragraph. “liwen” = leben; “hewen” = haben once again; “ere / eren” = ihre / ihrem. Her Schriften — papers, documents — are an errand the tale needs and does not explain.

sentences.t: Da werd de Ferenand getrü up Anstifften det Ferenand ungetrü roopen,
sentences.l: Then Ferenand getrü is called at the instigation of Ferenand ungetrü,
sentences.i: Then Ferenand getrü was called for, at the instigation of Ferenand ungetrü,
sentences.n: “up Anstifften” = auf Anstiften, at the prompting of; “det” = des, a genitive. It is the second time the false Ferenand puts the true one in the way of death, and the tale is keeping count.

sentences.t: un de Künig bedütt ünn he sulle de Schriften van dem Schlotte halen, süst sull he sterwen.
sentences.l: and the king gives him to understand that he should fetch the writings from the castle, otherwise he should die.
sentences.i: and the king gave him to understand that he was to fetch the writings from the castle, or else die.
sentences.n: “süst” here is sonst, otherwise — earlier in this tale the same spelling was sollst, you shall. “bedüen” = bedeuten, to give someone to understand, in an older use than the modern “to mean.”

sentences.t: Da geit he wier in Stall, un grind un segd „o min lewe Schümmelken, nu sull ik noch ’n mal weg, wie süll wie dat macken?“
sentences.l: Then he goes again into the stable and weeps and says “oh my dear little white horse, now I am to go off once more, how shall we do that?”
sentences.i: So he went into the stable again and wept and said: “Oh my dear little horse, now I must go off once more — how shall we manage it?”
sentences.n: “wie süll wie” = wie sollen wir: the first wie is “how,” the second is “we.” Man and horse have become a “we” by now, and the tale says so in a single word.

sentences.t: Da segd de Schümmel se sullen dat Schipp man wier vull laen (laden).
sentences.l: Then the white horse says they should just load the ship full again.
sentences.i: Then the horse said they need only load the ship full again.
sentences.n: “(laden)” is the Grimms’ own gloss on the dialect laen — to load. “man” again for nur, only.

sentences.t: Da geht es wieder wie das vorigemal, und die Riesen und die Vögel werden von dem Fleisch gesättigt und besänftigt.
sentences.l: Then it goes again as the previous time, and the giants and the birds are sated and appeased by the meat.
sentences.i: Then it went as it had the time before, and the giants and the birds were fed full with the meat and appeased.
sentences.n: High German again for this summarising sentence — and it is a summary: rather than repeat the charm a second time, the tale simply says that it went as before.

sentences.t: Ase se bie dat Schlott kümmet, segd de Schümmel to ünn he sulle man herin gahn, in den Schlapzimmer der Prinzessin, up den Diske da lägen de Schriften.
sentences.l: When they come to the castle, the white horse says to him he should just go in, into the princess’s bedchamber; on the table there the writings were lying.
sentences.i: When they came to the castle, the horse told him he need only go inside, into the princess’s bedchamber: the writings were lying there on the table.
sentences.n: “lägen” is the subjunctive of reported speech — the horse says where they are, and the German marks that it is the horse saying it. “Schlapzimmer” = Schlafzimmer; “Diske” = Tische.

sentences.t: Da geit Ferenand getrü hün un langet se.
sentences.l: Then Ferenand getrü goes there and fetches them.
sentences.i: So Ferenand getrü went and fetched them.
sentences.n: “langen” in Low German is to reach for, to fetch; the word comes back a few lines later, when the fish hands the quill over.

sentences.t: Ase se up’n Water sind, da let he sine Schriffedder in’t Water fallen, da segd de Schümmel „nu kann ik die awerst nig helpen.“
sentences.l: When they are on the water, he lets his writing-quill fall into the water, and the white horse says “now I cannot help you.”
sentences.i: When they were out on the water, he let his quill fall into the water, and the horse said: “Now I cannot help you.”
sentences.n: The quill he nearly left lying in the road at the beginning now falls where only the fish can reach it; the tale ties its two favours together and says nothing about the knot. “let” = ließ.

sentences.t: Da fällt’n dat bie mit de Flötepiepen, he fänkt an to flöten, da kümmt de Fisk un het de Fedder im Mule un langet se’m hen.
sentences.l: Then it occurs to him about the little flute; he begins to pipe, and the fish comes and has the quill in its mouth and hands it to him.
sentences.i: Then he remembered the little flute; he began to pipe, and the fish came with the quill in its mouth and handed it to him.
sentences.n: “fällt’n dat bie” = fällt ihm das bei — beifallen, where a thing “falls in” to a person, that is, occurs to him. “se’m” is se + ’m, sie ihm; that ’m is ihm here, not the clipped zusammen it stands for elsewhere. “Mule” = Maule.

sentences.t: Nu bringet he de Schriften na dem Schlotte, wo de Hochtid hallen werd.
sentences.l: Now he brings the writings to the castle, where the wedding is held.
sentences.i: Now he brought the writings to the castle, where the wedding was held.
sentences.n: “Hochtid” = Hochzeit; “hallen” = gehalten. The wedding goes by in half a line — the tale is not finished with these people yet.

sentences.t: De Künigin mogte awerst den Künig nig lien, weil he keine Nese hadde, sonnern se mogte den Ferenand getrü geren lien.
sentences.l: But the queen could not bear the king, because he had no nose, but she liked Ferenand getrü well.
sentences.i: But the queen could not bear the king, because he had no nose; Ferenand getrü she liked well.
sentences.n: “nig lien mögen” = nicht leiden mögen, to be unable to stand someone. The king’s missing nose arrives here without warning and is never explained anywhere in the tale; it is worth saying plainly that no one knows what it is doing there.

sentences.t: Wie nu mal alle Herens vom Hove tosammen sied, so segd de Künigin, se könne auck Kunststücke macken,
sentences.l: When now all the lords of the court are together, the queen says she could do tricks too,
sentences.i: One day, when all the lords of the court were together, the queen said that she too could do tricks,
sentences.n: “Herens” = Herren; “Hove” = Hofe, the court; “sied” = sind. “Kunststücke” are feats of art or conjuring — the same Kunst that means a craftsman’s skill.

sentences.t: se künne einen den Kopp afhoggen un wier upsetten, et sull nur mant einer versöcken.
sentences.l: she could hew a person’s head off and set it on again, only let someone try it.
sentences.i: she could strike a man’s head off and set it on again — let one of them only try it.
sentences.n: “einen den Kopp afhoggen” puts the person in the accusative and the head under a plain article: the case, not a possessive, says whose head it is. “mant” is a small particle of urging, roughly “just, only”; its exact force is not certainly explained. “versöcken” = versuchen.

sentences.t: Da wull awerst kener de eiste sien, da mott Ferenand getrü daran, wier up Anstifften von Ferenand ungetrü,
sentences.l: But no one wanted to be the first, so Ferenand getrü must to it, again at the instigation of Ferenand ungetrü,
sentences.i: But no one would be the first, so Ferenand getrü had to go through with it, again at the instigation of Ferenand ungetrü,
sentences.n: “mott … daran” — “must at it”: after müssen the verb of going is left out altogether, which German does whenever the direction is clear. “kener” = keiner; “eiste” = erste.

sentences.t: den hogget se den Kopp af un sett’n ünn auck wier up,
sentences.l: his head she hews off and sets it on him again too,
sentences.i: so she struck his head off and set it on him again,
sentences.n: “den” is the demonstrative in the dative — “to that one,” meaning him. “hogget … af” = haut ab; “sett’n” = setzt ihn, with the pronoun swallowed into the verb.

sentences.t: et is auck glick wier tau heilt, dat et ut sach ase hädde he ’n roen Faen (Faden) üm ’n Hals.
sentences.l: and it is at once healed up again, so that it looked as if he had a red thread around his neck.
sentences.i: and at once it was healed up again, so that it looked as though he had a red thread about his neck.
sentences.n: “(Faden)” is the Grimms’ own gloss on Faen, thread — the colour word roen (roten) beside it is not glossed, and is ours to explain. “tau heilt” = zugeheilt, healed shut; “glick” = gleich, at once. The red thread is the only trace the trick leaves, and it is the detail the tale wants remembered.

sentences.t: Da segd de Künig to ehr „mein Kind, wo hast du denn das gelernt?“
sentences.l: Then the king says to her “my child, where did you learn that?”
sentences.i: Then the king said to her: “My child, where did you learn that?”
sentences.n: The king speaks High German, as the court does throughout — the dialect belongs to the telling and to Ferenand getrü. “wo” for where, in the sense of from whom or by what means.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ segd se, „die Kunst versteh ich, soll ich es an dir auch einmal versuchen?“
sentences.l: “Yes,” says she, “that art I understand, shall I try it on you too, for once?”
sentences.i: “Yes,” she said, “I know that art — shall I try it on you as well?”
sentences.n: “die Kunst versteh ich” puts the object first: that art, I understand. The question is asked in the mildest words available, and the king is about to say yes.

sentences.t: „O ja“ segd he.
sentences.l: “Oh yes,” says he.
sentences.n: Two words, and the end of him; the tale spends nothing at all on the moment of decision.

sentences.t: Do hogget se en awerst den Kopp af un sett’n en nig wier upp,
sentences.l: Then she hews his head off but does not set it on him again,
sentences.i: So she struck his head off, but she did not set it on again,
sentences.n: The same words as before with “nig” — not — dropped into the middle: the sentence that healed the servant kills the king. “upp” here is the particle auf, belonging to upsetten.

sentences.t: se doet as ob se’n nig darup kriegen künne, un as ob he nig fest sitten wulle.
sentences.l: she does as if she could not get it on again, and as if it would not sit firm.
sentences.i: she made as though she could not get it back on, and as though it would not sit firm.
sentences.n: “doet as ob” = tut als ob, makes as if; the subjunctives künne and wulle mark the pretence. The murder is committed by acting badly on purpose, and the tale reports it without comment.

sentences.t: Da werd de Künig begrawen, se awerst frigget den Ferenand getrü.
sentences.l: Then the king is buried, but she marries Ferenand getrü.
sentences.i: So the king was buried, and she married Ferenand getrü.
sentences.n: “frigget” = freit, from freien, to woo or to marry; the woman is the subject of it here, and the tale does not remark on that either.

sentences.t: He ride awerst jümmer sinen Schümmel, un ase he mal darup sat,
sentences.l: But he always rode his white horse, and when he sat on it once,
sentences.i: But he always rode his white horse, and once when he was sitting on it,
sentences.n: “ride” = ritt, rode. After everything at court, the tale turns back to the horse — which is where it has been going all along.

sentences.t: da segd he to em he sulle mal up ’ne annere Heide de he em wist, trecken un da dreimal mit em herumme jagen.
sentences.l: then it said to him he should ride onto another heath, which it showed him, and gallop round there three times with it.
sentences.i: the horse said to him that he should ride out onto another heath, which it showed him, and gallop round it three times.
sentences.n: Both he and em stand for rider and for horse in this one sentence, and only the sense sorts them out: it is the horse that speaks and shows the heath. “wist” = wies, showed; “herumme jagen” = herumjagen. The tale ends where it began, on a heath.

sentences.t: Wie he dat dahen hadde, da geit de Schümmel up de Hinnerbeine stahn un verwannelt sik in ’n Künigssuhn.
sentences.l: When he had done that, the white horse goes to stand on its hind legs and changes itself into a king’s son.
sentences.i: When he had done that, the horse stood up on its hind legs and changed into a king’s son.
sentences.n: “dahen” = gethan (modern getan); “verwannelt sik” = verwandelt sich. The tale stops here, with no word about who had enchanted the horse or why — the ending is exactly this abrupt in the 1857 text.

glossary.becker: Low German: der Bäcker — bakers (pl.; ‘alle Becker’ = alle Bäcker)
glossary.been: anbieten — offers (‘been sik an’ = bietet sich an, offers himself; Low German been = bieten, not Bein, a leg)
glossary.dacht: denken — gedacht, thought (past participle; Low German = gedacht)
glossary.die: Low German: dir, dich — (to) you (‘ik will die helpen’ = ich will dir helfen); the article die also appears, in this tale’s High German passages
glossary.döre: durch — through, by means of (Low German)
glossary.er: Low German: ihr — (to) her (‘segd er’ = sagte ihr); in this tale’s High German passages also er — he
glossary.es: es — it (the impersonal es of this tale’s High German passages)
glossary.flöten: flöten — to pipe, blow the flute (infinitive; ‘fänkt an to flöten’ = fängt an zu flöten)
glossary.fragen: das Fragen — the asking (infinitive used as a noun; ‘dat Fragen’ = das Fragen)
glossary.grauten: Low German: groß — great, big (adj., infl.; here nom./acc. pl., ‘de grauten Riesen’)
glossary.hab: haben — hab, I have (1st sg., clipped from habe; ‘ich hab euch was mitgebracht’)
glossary.hewen: haben — to have (Low German hewen/hebben; ‘se möste ere Schriften hewen’ = sie müßte ihre Schriften haben)
glossary.hören: hören — to belong (Low German for gehören; ‘dat sulle em hören’ = das sollte ihm gehören); also hören — to hear
glossary.ihm: ihm — to him (dative; in this tale’s High German passages)
glossary.jagen: jagen — to gallop, race (infinitive; ‘herumme jagen’ = herumjagen, to gallop about); also to hunt, chase
glossary.jagt: jagen — jagt, races, gallops (3rd sg.; the Grimms’ own gloss in their text on the dialect jegd)
glossary.jungen: der Junge — boy (acc. sg.; ‘en kleinen Jungen’ = einen kleinen Jungen)
glossary.kinne: das Kind — child (dat. sg.; Low German Kinne; ‘dem Kinne nix giwen’ = dem Kinde nichts geben)
glossary.laden: laden — to load (the Grimms’ own gloss in their text on the dialect laen; not der Laden, a shop)
glossary.lett: Low German: läßt — lets, has (a thing) done (laten = lassen, 3rd sg.; ‘da lett de Künig … slachten’)
glossary.m: ’m — ihm, to him (‘langet se’m hen’ = langt sie ihm hin)
glossary.mal: mal — once, at some time (adverbial einmal; ‘he wulle mal … gahn’ = er wollte einmal … gehen)
glossary.man: Low German: man — only, just (‘gah man hen’ = geh nur hin; not the impersonal High German man, ‘one’)
glossary.midde: mit — with, along (Low German; ‘midde bringen’ = mitbringen, to bring along)
glossary.n: ’n — ein, einen, a (‘’n Perd’ = ein Pferd); also = ihn, him (‘gript ’n’ = greift ihn); in ‘up’n’ = auf den
glossary.nah: Low German: nach — to, toward (variant of na; ‘nah Hus’ = nach Haus)
glossary.schicken: schicken — to send (‘den schicken Sie hin’ = schicken Sie ihn hin)
glossary.schippe: Low German: das Schiff — ships (pl. Schippe)
glossary.sett: Low German: setzt — sets (3rd sg. pres.; ‘he sik darup sett’ = er sich darauf setzt)
glossary.sied: Low German: sind, seid — are (‘gi sied arm’ = ihr seid arm; ‘wie se vull sied’ = wie sie voll sind)
glossary.sin: Low German: sein — to be; bin, am (‘wat sin ik’ = was bin ich); also sein — his (possessive)
glossary.süll: Low German: sollen — shall, are to (‘wie süll wie dat macken’ = wie sollen wir das machen)
glossary.t: ’t — the reduced form of dat, the (‘in’t Water’ = in das Wasser); elsewhere also et, it
glossary.treck: Low German: zieh — come along, go (ziehen, imper.; ‘treck mit mie in’t Schipp’ = zieh mit mir ins Schiff)
glossary.upp: Low German: up — on, up (the particle of upsetten: ‘sett’n … wier upp’ = setzte ihn wieder auf)
glossary.wahren: wahren, bewahren — to keep, hold on to (‘tom Frünne wahren’ = sich zum Freunde bewahren)
glossary.west: Low German: gewesen — been (‘’ne Fru west’ = eine Frau gewesen); also west du = weißt du, do you know
glossary.wie: Low German: wir — we (‘wie süll wie dat macken’); also wie — how, as, when
glossary.wust: wissen — wußte, knew (3rd sg. past; Low German)
glossary.üm: Low German: ihm — (to) him (‘hinner üm’ = hinter ihm); also üm = um, around (‘üm ’n Hals’ = um den Hals)
